output.query: exercise triggered migraine aura confusional aura marathon dehydration CSD

results.finding: Aerobic exercise triggers migraine via dehydration/hypoglycaemia, hyperventilation, adenosine release, and CSD susceptibility during metabolic stress. ICHD-3 recognises migraine with confusional aura — transient confusion/amnesia as aura; more common in young adults; resolves within 30-60 min. Dehydration, hyponatraemia, and hypoglycaemia at 15km in a half-marathon are all CSD triggers converging. Most exercise-triggered migraine resolves spontaneously; preventive during race season may be considered.

output.query: migraine prevention endurance athlete marathon propranolol topiramate CGRP

results.finding: Hydration is the most critical intervention; target pre-race weight maintenance with electrolyte sports drink; prevent >2% body weight loss. Carbohydrate loading (7-10 g/kg/day for 3 days pre-race) prevents glycogen depletion-triggered CSD. Caffeine: withdrawal headache if stopped before race; consistent daily intake reduces risk. Beta-blockers (propranolol) REDUCE exercise tolerance — avoid in competitive athletes. Topiramate 25-50 mg/day does not impair exercise performance. Anti-CGRP antibodies show no exercise limitation. Naratriptan (longer half-life) may be used at headache onset.

output.summary: For exercise-related headache and aura, hydration and carbohydrate loading are emphasised; beta-blockers are avoided in competitive athletes (reduce exercise tolerance); topiramate or CGRP antibodies are athlete-compatible preventive options

output.query: PRES posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome exertional migraine differential

results.finding: PRES: typically associated with hypertensive emergency, immunosuppressive agents, or eclampsia; MRI shows posterior white matter T2/FLAIR signal change. In the absence of posterior FLAIR signal change on MRI, PRES is not supported. Exertion-induced hypertension could theoretically cause PRES in susceptible individuals, but normal resting BP and normal MRI argues against this. Primary exertional headache (ICHD-3 4.2) is characteristically bilateral without aura; unilateral spreading visual aura with subsequent headache is characteristic of migraine with aura.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 27-year-old British man was referred to the neurology outpatient clinic following an alarming episode 4 weeks ago. He was running during a half-marathon event when, at approximately the 15-kilometre mark, he noticed a flickering haze appear in his right peripheral vision that expanded over approximately 20 minutes into a typical zigzag shimmering arc. He slowed to a walk. During the aura, he also felt confused and disoriented — he didn't recognise other runners around him and couldn't recall his race number momentarily. A St John Ambulance volunteer was called. The visual aura and confusion resolved within 30-35 minutes. He was assessed briefly at the event and was found alert and oriented at that time. Approximately 20 minutes later, he developed a severe bilateral throbbing headache (9/10) with nausea and intense photophobia that lasted approximately 14 hours. He was taken to A&E where he was given IV fluids for dehydration.

He had never had a visual aura before and no prior significant headaches. He completed a head CT in A&E which was reported as normal. He is an active marathon runner (training 50-60 km/week). He is healthy, takes no medications, has no medical history, and no family history of epilepsy. His older sister has migraines without aura. He consumes caffeine strategically around training and does not drink alcohol. He specifically denies any weakness, speech difficulty, or loss of consciousness during or after the episode. He is extremely anxious about exercising again.
